newsitem.title: USA: Gold slide continues as funds flood into U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: Gold slide continues as funds flood into U.S. stocks.

text.p: Gold prices fell to a 20-month low Monday as investors continued to pour funds into the surging stock market and neglected the struggling precious metal.

"We may be about to see a climactic sell-off in gold as investment is sucked away into what could be a once-in-a-lifetime, blow-off rally in the stock market," said John Brimelow, New York director of international equities for BV Capital.
Oil prices fell on news that Iraq had agreed to all U.N. conditions in an oil-for-food deal and that the deal could be implemented by the end of the year.
Weaker gold and oil prices contributed to a fall of 0.88 point to 243.31 points in the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts.

On New York's Comex December gold ended down $1.80 an ounce at $374.50 after posting a contract low at $373.40, while spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted at $374.35/374.85 an ounce after dipping to a 20-month low around $373.00.

"Extraordinary upward momentum in equity markets, more sustained gains in bond prices, a softer-than-anticipated seasonal upturn in physical demand and prospects of producer forward selling are keeping gold prices on the defensive," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
Oil losses were contained by the fact that the Iraqi news was to some extent already reflected in prices following reports last week that a deal could be near at hand.
"A lot of this news was already in the marketplace," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil.

Crude for January delivery finished 26 cents lower at $23.49 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, while December heating oil ended 0.56 cent lower a gallon at 72.33 cents. December gasoline resisted crude's declines and ended up 0.19 cent a gallon at 67.99 cents.
Under the deal, the United Nations would lift certain sanctions against Iraq and that nation would be allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil in exchange for humanitarian aid.

Traders said high demand for heating oil due to cold weather in Europe and the United States and increasing use of oil by developing countries should easily absorb the increase in supply from the Iraqi oil deal.
"This crude would be coming at a great time," said Samuels.

"We are living at a hand-to-mouth existence with heating oil amid winter, so crude stocks will be needed for heating oil output," Samuels said. Heating oil stocks are 15 million barrels below a year ago, according to the most recent oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute.

Traders and analysts also took a wait-and-see view of developments in the oil deal since disagreement between the United States and Iraq over how the deal will be carried out has caused several delays.
"I'm still pretty sceptical," said Tom Bentz, analyst with ING Derivatives.
Still, crude prices initially lost 50 cents when Iraqi U.N. Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon said Baghdad had agreed to the deal's conditionsl.
American U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright said the United States was "very pleased" and that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali appeared ready to put the deal into effect.
She also said the United States expected to approve an oil pricing formula covering Iraqi oil contracts when it goes before the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee.
The deal was signed last May and was about to be implemented when Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq in late August to support one side of a Kurdish conflict.
